title: MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ incelemesi: Güçlü el konsolu yüksek fiyatla geliyor
summary: Stuff'ın incelemesine göre MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ yüksek performans ve pil ömrü sunuyor ancak yüksek fiyatı ve OLED ekran bulunmaması dezavantaj yaratıyor.
body:
Stuff dergisinin incelemesine göre taşınabilir oyuncu pazarındaki yeni **MSI Claw 8 EX AI+**, gelişmiş donanımıyla dikkat çeken iddialı bir el konsolu olarak öne çıkıyor. Intel işlemci ve Arc G3 grafik biriminden güç alan cihaz, sunduğu yüksek performans ve uzun pil ömrüyle rakiplerine meydan okuyor.

## Tasarım ve ekran özellikleri

Cihaz, mor ve siyah renklerin bir arada kullanıldığı dikkat çekici gövde tasarımıyla geliyor. 785 gram ağırlığındaki el konsolu, selefine kıyasla daha konforlu bir tutuş sunacak şekilde yenilenmiş ergonomik tutma yerlerine sahip. 8 inç büyüklüğündeki 1920x1200 piksel çözünürlük sunan LCD ekranı 48-120Hz değişken yenileme hızı destekliyor ve 500 nit tepe parlaklığa ulaşabiliyor. Ancak yüksek fiyat etiketine rağmen OLED ekran ve HDR desteğinin bulunmaması eleştiriliyor.

## Performans ve fiyat

Donanım tarafında Hall efekt sensörlü analog çubuklar ve tetikler kullanılarak çubuk kayması sorununun önüne geçilmiş. Windows 11 tabanlı sistemde MSI Centre M yazılımı yer alıyor. Yüksek bileşen maliyetleri nedeniyle Amerika'da 1799 dolar, İngiltere'de ise 1449 pound gibi yüksek bir fiyatla satışa sunuluyor.

**Neden önemli?** Güçlü performans ve pil ömrüne sahip olan MSI Claw 8 EX AI+, yüksek fiyatı nedeniyle ortalama bir oyuncunun bütçesini zorlayabilecek bir konumda yer alıyor.

source_texts.title: The MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ is a gloriously potent gaming handheld – I just wish the price wasn’t so painful
source_texts.summary: Intel's Arc G3 Extreme delivers serious oomph in a small package
source_texts.text:
Stuff Verdict
A brilliantly powerful handheld with great battery life and strong ergonomics, but the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ is tricky to love on account of the prohibitive asking price
Pros
- Comfortably the most powerful PC-based handheld out there
- Very respectable battery life
- Comfortable to hold with ergonomic controls
Cons
- Lack of OLED screen is disappointing
- Bonkers price
- It’s very big
Introduction
The Claw 8 EX AI+ is a gaming handheld on a redemption tour. Not just for its maker MSI, whose earlier efforts made a few questionable ergonomic choices, but also for chipmaker Intel; the firm’s old Lunar Lake silicon couldn’t compete with AMD’s Ryzen Z1, which basically had the class all to itself. Arc G3 wants to be the seriously rapid yet impressively efficient follow-up that redresses the balance.
Things looked promising in my early taster session at Taiwan’s Computex show, but now that the final retail version has landed, Intel wasn’t blowing smoke – the Claw 8 EX AI+ really does have the muscle to embarrass the Asus Xbox ROG Ally X and the stamina to do so for an impressive length of time on battery power.
The only problem? An all-new processor plus copious amounts of RAM and flash storage, at a time when high demand has sent component costs sky-high, means you’ll need to shell out $1799/£1449 to take one home. That’s a colossal jump from the Steam Deck OLED, as well as virtually every AMD-powered handheld. Does that make it impossible for the average gamer to justify?
How we test gaming hardware
All games consoles and gaming hardware tested on Stuff are put through their paces with days’ worth of play time. We use our years of testing experience to judge areas such as build quality, software experience, battery life and other features. Manufacturers have no visibility on reviews before they appear online, and we never accept payment to feature products.
Find out more about how we test and rate products.
Where has MSI streamlined the Claw 8 EX AI+’s design?
I hope you like purple, as the Claw 8 EX AI+ only comes in that one distinctive hue. I’m a fan – it instantly sets the MSI apart from rivals like the Steam Deck and Lenovo Legion Go 2, but without being as shouty as the Xbox ROG Ally X20‘s translucent gold. That is, until the RGB illumination around the analogue sticks kicks into life. Besides, only the top half is purple; it’s black underneath, with MSI’s signature dragon crest sandwiched between two large fan grilles that mean business.
MSI’s older handhelds had blocky grips that weren’t all that comfortable to wrap your hands around, so I was relieved to see the firm refine its ergonomics for 2026. The Claw 8 EX AI+ has a more sculpted shape, with chunkier grips that better fill your palms but don’t move the controls out of reach. There are textured portions where you need them the most and weight distribution is pretty good.
The Claw weighs a substantial 785g, which may be less than the previous generation, but is still over 100g than a Steam Deck OLED. I still found it comfy enough to use for hours at a time, but you’re definitely paying a penalty for that larger display.
Connectivity is largely unchanged from the last Claw, with a pair of USB-C ports up top alongside a microSD card slot, 3.5mm headphone port and a power button that doubles as a reasonably quick and accurate fingerprint sensor. The USB ports tick along at Thunderbolt 4 speeds and the card slot swallows faster microSD Express cards, which is great news for anyone with large game collections or the desire to hook up to an external display.
Six Phillips-head screws secure the rear panel, should you want to upgrade the single 2280 PCIe 4.0 SSD later down the line.
What are the Claw 8’s inputs like to use?
MSI hasn’t broken the mould in terms of button layout here, keeping the same rough placement as its earlier Claw efforts. You get an Xbox-style offset analogue stick setup; the standard four face buttons; an eight-way D-pad; and two sets of triggers and bumpers up top. There are also two customisable buttons on the rear of the handheld.
Almost every input has tweaked or redesigned for the better, though. The analogue sticks use Hall effect sensors instead of physical contacts, fully preventing the possibility of stick drift over time. The face buttons aren’t as mushy as previous efforts, with a more responsive and clicky action (without actually using mouse-like microswitches), and the D-pad has much more distinctive four-way directions. The shape is great for multi-direction fighting game inputs too.
I found the bumpers easier to reach than the smaller Acer Predator Atlas 7 I tried at IFA earlier in the year, with a crisp click that instantly lets you know an input has registered. The triggers also use Hall effect tech and have a good amount of resistance. You miss out on the Impulse trigger rumble effects seen on the Xbox Ally X, but haptics in general are substantial.
Does the Claw 8’s screen stand out?
Quite literally, yes – the display’s bottom edge pokes outwards from the main chassis in order to accommodate its sizeable 8in diagonal. It’s thick enough to let the device stand upright quite firmly, which could be handy for hands-free video playback. Reasonably skinny bezels mean it fills more of the available space than an ROG Ally does and the 16:10 aspect ratio is a little taller too.
The 1920×1200 resolution has the Asus beaten for pixel count, along with the Steam Deck OLED. It looks satisfyingly crisp without asking too much of the GPU, like the original Legion Go did. A 48-120Hz variable refresh rate keeps games looking smooth in pretty much all situations.
It’s an LCD panel underneath, though, which is disappointing given the high price. While the Claw has colours that are fairly impactful for the tech, they’re still in second place compared to an OLED – which also takes a commanding lead for contrast and shadow definition. Viewing angles are decent rather than fantastic too.
A peak 500 nits brightness I was still able to play darker game levels without having to draw the curtains, in spite of the very glossy finish highlighting reflections all too easily. There’s no HDR support here either: compatible titles look so much more dynamic and engaging on rivals like the Steam Deck OLED, whereas here you’re stuck with standard dynamic range.
It’s not a bad screen overall, but I’d rather have an OLED with HDR even if it meant accepting a slightly lower resolution.
I thought the integrated speakers were a great pairing to the display, at least, with ample volume and good overall clarity. There’s little in the way of meaty bass, of course, and high frequencies are at the edge of bring shrill or tinny at extreme volumes. I’d usually reach for a pair of headphones for anything beyond casual gaming.
